'''Jonathan Felix Ashmore''' (born 1948)<ref name=whoswho /> is a British [[physicist]] and [[Bernard Katz]] Professor of [[Biophysics]] at [[University College London]].<ref name=uclacuk>{{cite web|url=https://www.ucl.ac.uk/ear/research/pi/ashmorelab |title=Professor Jonathan Ashmore Lab Page |website=ucl.ac.uk|publisher=University College London |date=2017 |access-date=25 April 2017|author=Anon|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170426055617/https://www.ucl.ac.uk/ear/research/pi/ashmorelab|archive-date=26 April 2017}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
Ashmore is the son of theatre director and actor [[Peter Ashmore (theatre director and actor)|Peter Ashmore]] and the actress [[Rosalie Crutchley]].<ref>{{Cite news |last=Purser |first=Philip |date=20 August 1997 |title=The Director's Cut, Guardian Obituary, Peter Ashmore |url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/260782911/?terms=peter%20ashmore%20&match=1 |access-date=9 April 2024 |work=[[The Guardian newspaper]] |pages=16}}</ref>

Aged seven, Ashmore played Joe in the 1955 film ''[[A Kid for Two Farthings (film)|A Kid for Two Farthings]]'', adapted from [[A Kid for Two Farthings (novel)|the novel]] by [[Wolf Mankowitz]].<ref name=imdb>{{IMDb name|0039155 }}</ref>

Educated at [[Westminster School]]<ref name=whoswho>{{Who's Who | title=ASHMORE, Prof. Jonathan Felix | id = U5847 | volume = 2017 | edition = online [[Oxford University Press]]|location=Oxford}}</ref> as a [[Queen's Scholar (Westminster School)|Queen's Scholar]], Ashmore studied mathematics and physics at the [[University of Sussex]]<ref name=orcid>{{ORCID|0000-0001-6522-3692}}</ref> followed by a [[PhD]] in [[theoretical physics]] in 1971 supervised by [[Tom Kibble]] at [[Imperial College London]] where his research investigated [[quantum field theory]].<ref name=ashphd>{{cite thesis|degree=PhD|publisher=University of London|title=Aspects of quantum field theory|first=Jonathan Felix|last=Ashmore|date=1972|url=http://ethos.bl.uk/OrderDetails.do?uin=uk.bl.ethos.623991|website=ethos.bl.uk|oclc=930651621|hdl=10044/1/16203}}{{dead link|date=December 2023 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>

== Career and research ==
After a short [[postdoctoral]] [[research fellow]]ship supervised by [[Abdus Salam]]<ref name=rsbm /> at the [[International Centre for Theoretical Physics]] in [[Trieste]], Italy he retrained as a physiologist at UCL, gaining a [[Master of Science]] degree in 1974<ref name=orcid /> which led to work with [[Paul Fatt]] and [[Gertrude Falk]]<ref name=falk>{{cite web|author=Anon|year=2008|url=http://www.dcscience.net/Gertrude-Falk-obituary-PhysSoclb.pdf|title=Physiological Society obituary: Gertrude Falk 1925–2008|website=dcscienece.net}}</ref> between 1974 and 1977 in the Biophysics Department.

Ashmore was appointed a [[Lecturer]] in [[Physiology]] at the [[University of Bristol]] in 1983 and promoted to [[Reader (academic rank)|Reader]] in 1988, before moving back to UCL in 1993.<ref name=rsbm /><ref name=orcid />

Ashmore has worked on dissecting the cellular mechanisms of hearing by studying the [[organ of Corti]] in the mammalian [[cochlea]]<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Housley|first1=G. D.|last2=Ashmore|first2=J. F.|date=1991|title=Direct Measurement of the Action of Acetylcholine on Isolated Outer Hair Cells of the Guinea Pig Cochlea|journal=Proceedings of the Royal Society of London B: Biological Sciences|language=en|volume=244|issue=1310|pages=161–167|doi=10.1098/rspb.1991.0065|issn=0962-8452|pmid=1679550|bibcode=1991RSPSB.244..161H|s2cid=1950263}}</ref> especially the [[guinea pig]] (''Cavia porcellus'').<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Ashmore|first1=J. F.|last2=Meech|first2=R. W.|date=1986|title=Ionic basis of membrane potential in outer hair cells of guinea pig cochlea|pmid= 2426595 |journal=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]|language=en|volume=322|issue=6077|pages=368–371|doi=10.1038/322368a0|bibcode=1986Natur.322..368A|s2cid=4371640}} {{closed access}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Nobili|first1=Renato|last2=Mammano|first2=Fabio|last3=Ashmore|first3=Jonathan|date=1998|title=How well do we understand the cochlea?|journal=Trends in Neurosciences|volume=21|issue=4|pages=159–167|doi=10.1016/s0166-2236(97)01192-2|pmid=9554726|s2cid=15474808|hdl=11577/2461756|hdl-access=free}} {{closed access}}</ref> This structure in the inner ear increases the selectivity and sensitivity of our hearing through an in-built [[cochlear amplifier]].<ref name=frs /> He showed that specialised cells known as [[outer hair cell]]s are responsible for this unique function.<ref name=frs /><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Ashmore|first=Jonathan Felix|year=1987|title=A fast motile response in guinea-pig outer hair cells: the cellular basis of the cochlear amplifier|journal=[[The Journal of Physiology]]|language=en|volume=388|issue=1|pages=323–347|doi=10.1113/jphysiol.1987.sp016617|issn=1469-7793|pmid=3656195 |pmc=1192551}} {{open access}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Ashmore|first=Jonathan|date=2008|title=Cochlear Outer Hair Cell Motility|journal=[[Physiological Reviews]]|language=en|volume=88|issue=1|pages=173–210|doi=10.1152/physrev.00044.2006|issn=0031-9333|pmid= 18195086}} {{open access}}</ref>

In response to sound, outer hair cells lengthen then shorten through a process controlled and powered by the flow of electrically charged molecules such as [[potassium]] [[ion]]s.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Housley|first1=G D|last2=Ashmore|first2=J F|date=1992|title=Ionic currents of outer hair cells isolated from the guinea-pig cochlea.|pmid=1593487 |pmc=1176188|journal=[[The Journal of Physiology]]|language=en|volume=448|issue=1|pages=73–98|doi=10.1113/jphysiol.1992.sp019030|issn=1469-7793}} {{open access}}</ref> This contraction propagates and amplifies sound, and he was the first to capture it on film during his ''[[Rock Around the Clock]] Hair Cell'' video.<ref name=uclacuk /><ref name=frs />

His work has combined biophysical methods – including the [[patch clamp]] technique usually applied to [[membrane protein]]s – with [[confocal microscopy]] imaging and [[computational model]]ling to expand our knowledge of hearing at the molecular and cellular level. His findings are helping to unravel the nature and origins of hearing-related conditions like [[deafness]] and [[tinnitus]].<ref name=croonian /><ref name=frs>{{cite web|author=Anon|year=1996|title=Professor Jonathan Ashmore FMedSci FRS|website=royalsociety.org|publisher=[[Royal Society]]|location=London|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151117003552/https://royalsociety.org/people/jonathan-ashmore-11009/|url=https://royalsociety.org/people/jonathan-ashmore-11009/|archive-date=17 November 2015}} One or more of the preceding sentences incorporates text from the royalsociety.org website where: {{blockquote|"All text published under the heading 'Biography' on Fellow profile pages is available under [[Creative Commons license|Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License]]." --{{cite web |url=https://royalsociety.org/about-us/terms-conditions-policies/ |title=Royal Society Terms, conditions and policies |access-date=2016-03-09 |url-status=bot: unknown |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161111170346/https://royalsociety.org/about-us/terms-conditions-policies/ |archive-date=2016-11-11 }}}}</ref>

His research has been funded by the [[Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council]] (BBSRC) and the [[Medical Research Council (United Kingdom)|Medical Research Council (MRC)]]<ref name=grants>{{cite web|author=Anon|year=2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171031131907/http://gtr.rcuk.ac.uk/person/4F167754-DA3F-476D-A1E3-06C3DF342BF3|archive-date=31 October 2017|url=http://gtr.rcuk.ac.uk/person/4F167754-DA3F-476D-A1E3-06C3DF342BF3|website=gtr.rcuk.ac.uk|location=Swindon|publisher=[[Research Councils UK]]|title=UK Government Grants awarded to Jonathan Ashmore}}</ref> and he has supervised several doctoral students to completion including Dan Jagger.<ref name=dagger>{{cite thesis|degree=PhD|publisher=University of Bristol|title=	Modulation of ion channels in outer hair cells from the mammalian cochlea|first= Daniel James|last=Jagger|date=1996|url=http://ethos.bl.uk/OrderDetails.do?uin=uk.bl.ethos.336876|website=ethos.bl.uk|oclc=931565011}}</ref>

=== Awards and honours ===
Ashmore was elected a [[Fellow of the Royal Society]] (FRS) in 1996<ref name=whoswho /> and gave their [[Croonian Lecture]] in 2017 on the [[neuroscience]] of [[deafness]].<ref name=croonian>Ashmore, Jonathan (2017) {{YouTube|id=GiZRlJl1eVw|title=Now you hear it, now you don't: the neuroscience of deafness}}</ref> He is also an elected [[Fellow of the Academy of Medical Sciences]] (FMedSci), a [[Fellow of the Royal Society of Biology]] (FRSB)<ref name=whoswho /> and a member of both the [[Association for Research in Otolaryngology]] and The [[Biophysical Society]].<ref name=f1000 />

Ashmore is [[Faculty of 1000]] section head for Sensory Systems<ref name=f1000>{{cite web |url=http://f1000.com/thefaculty/member/4033843402519366 |title=Jonathan Ashmore: Section Head in Sensory Systems – F1000Prime |website=F1000.com |author=Anon |year=2011 |access-date=25 April 2017 |archive-date=5 April 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120405193122/http://f1000.com/thefaculty/member/4033843402519366 |url-status=dead }}</ref>
and a trustee for the [[Deafness Research UK|Hearing Research Trust]].{{citation needed|date=October 2017}} He served as president of [[The Physiological Society]] from 2012 to 2014.<ref name=rsbm />

== Personal life ==
Through his mother, Ashmore is descended from the [[Thomas Coke, 1st Earl of Leicester (seventh creation)|1st Earl of Leicester]] and his second wife, Lady Anne Amelia Keppel, a descendant of [[Charles II of England]].
